title: Characters shared across species with very different habits indicate common inheritance

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Characters shared across species with very different habits indicate common inheritance

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: However trifling a character, if it occurs throughout many species with very different habits of life it can be explained only by inheritance from a common parent, and so has high value for classification; for the same reason rudimentary structures can be as useful as other parts.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. XIII: Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: if it prevail throughout many and different species, especially those having very different habits of life, it assumes high value; for we can account for its presence in so many forms with such different habits, only by its inheritance from a common parent.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter XIII, “Mutual Affinities of Organic Beings: Morphology: Embryology: Rudimentary Organs”; section “Descent always used in classification”. Scope: characters of animals and plants within large groups

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch13-07: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.62

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Independent molecular evidence can test common inheritance for many specific characters. Public morphology data are selective, and universal exclusion of convergence is not possible.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For shared morphological characters across ecologically divergent species, compare their distribution with independent molecular phylogenies and models of common inheritance versus convergence. Broad phylogenetic congruence despite habitat divergence supports inheritance and classificatory value.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The assertion 'only' is difficult to establish because convergence is always possible.

Trifling and rudimentary characters are inconsistently annotated.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
analysis feasibility: 0.55
data existence: 0.72
operationalizability: 0.68
discriminating power: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.5

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The contrast between cross-habit characters and habit-linked resemblances is a usable test of homology versus convergence, once habits are coded. Matrices and molecular trees exist for many vertebrate groups and some plants, not for animals and plants at large. The analysis is standard cladistic fit, slowed by the need to add habit annotations the matrices usually lack.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Code characters shared by many ecologically dissimilar species and ask whether those characters, including rudiments, match an independent molecular tree more often than characters shared by species with similar habits. The claim is confirmed if cross-habit characters are phylogenetically conserved and habit-linked similarities are homoplasious, and refuted if the reverse holds.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Rudimentary structures are mentioned sporadically in anatomical matrices rather than scored across whole classes.

Developmental constraint and gene transfer can spread a character across dissimilar species without inheritance from the group's common parent.

Habit categories in matrices are coarse, so 'very different habits' is only approximately known.

data adequacy: 0.5
